section_title: Will the people listen to the warning?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 19 Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We must have a king over us. 20 Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” 21 Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD. 22 “Listen to their voice,” the LORD said to Samuel. “Appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the men of Israel, “Everyone must go back to his city.”

context_lines: The warning does not change the people’s answer. They insist on having a king so they can be like the nations, with someone to judge them, lead them and fight their battles. Their desired outcome remains more compelling to them than Samuel’s explanation of its cost.

Samuel repeats their words before the LORD. God again tells him to listen and appoint a king. Samuel then sends the people home. The chapter ends with the request granted in principle, while the choice and appointment of the ruler still lie ahead.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) emphasizes the irony of seeking a military protector after God has just rescued Israel in response to prayer. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/8.htm) stresses their refusal to reconsider and the long consequences that can follow an insistent demand.

Both readings distinguish receiving a request from being right to make it. The command to appoint a king stands alongside God’s earlier description of rejection and Samuel’s warning. The text does not invite readers to erase either side of that account.
